page_title: In Praise of Memorization | Pearl Leff

summary.title: In Praise of Memorization
summary.one_liner: Memorizing facts gives you a mental scaffold for reasoning and organizing new information, so you can draw connections that looking things up alone won't reveal.
takeaways: Reasoning is limited by the facts you have at hand; you cannot connect things you do not know exist.
Memorized checkpoints (e.g., dates, places) give new information a place to attach and make it easier to remember.
Looking facts up in isolation tends to leave them jumbled and quickly forgotten.
Memorized material stays accessible over time and can be revisited and understood more deeply later.
summary.summary: The author recounts working with highly productive engineers who had built their knowledge by memorizing reference material in a pre-internet environment. The essay argues that memorization matters even though facts are easy to look up, because reasoning depends on having a bank of facts to test hypotheses against and a framework to attach new information to. It illustrates this with examples from geography (Oman and the Strait of Hormuz, Crimea and Russia's warm-water ports), dates (printing press and the Reformation, Daylight Saving Time and World War I), and a personal account of memorizing a poem in high school. It is an opinion essay with anecdotes rather than a technical guide.
